**How matching blocks are picked**

`get_matching_blocks` is greedy divide-and-conquer. It asks `find_longest_match` for the single longest contiguous block common to `a[alo:ahi]` and `b[blo:bhi]`, records it, then repeats on the region to the left of that block and the region to the right. The recursion is done with an explicit `queue`, so the blocks are sorted afterwards, adjacent ones are merged, and the `(len(a), len(b), 0)` sentinel is appended. Because the longest block is committed first and never revisited, the result is not a minimal edit script. Matches can never cross an earlier block, which is what keeps them in increasing order in both sequences.

`find_longest_match` walks `a` one element at a time. For each `a[i]` it looks up `b2j[a[i]]`, the list of positions where that element occurs in `b`, and sets `newj2len[j] = j2len.get(j-1, 0) + 1`. That is the length of the common run ending at `a[i]`, `b[j]`, built from the run that ended one step earlier in both. The best is only replaced on a strict `k > bestsize`, so ties go to the block starting earliest in `a`, then earliest in `b`. The cost is proportional to the number of (i, j) pairs with equal elements, which is why very common elements are expensive.

**What junk does**

If you pass `isjunk`, `__chain_b` deletes every junk element from `b2j` (and remembers them in `bjunk`). This has three consequences:

- **Junk cannot seed a match.** The loop above never sees a junk element, so the longest block is chosen among junk-free runs only.
- **Junk can still be absorbed.** After the seed is chosen, it is extended in both directions through matching non-junk, then through matching junk. So junk ends up in a block only when it sits next to an "interesting" match.
- **Junk-only regions mostly don't match.** If a sub-region has no seedable element in common, the seed is the empty block at `(alo, blo)`. Only elements that line up at the very start of both sub-regions get picked up; otherwise the region becomes a replace/insert/delete.

The docstring example shows the effect: with blanks as junk, `" abcd"` vs `"abcd abcd"` matches the leftmost `abcd` (size 4) instead of `" abcd"` at the tail (size 5). The junk test is applied only to `b`, so results (including `ratio()`) can change if you swap the arguments.

**What autojunk does**

When `autojunk=True` and `len(b) >= 200`, any non-junk element occurring more than `len(b) // 100 + 1` times in `b` is deemed "popular" and also deleted from `b2j`. Unlike real junk it is not put in `bjunk`. Popular elements therefore cannot seed a match either, but they are absorbed in the first (non-junk) extension pass rather than the second.

The intent is speed: for files with hundreds of blank lines or `return NULL;` lines, it removes the pairs that dominate the inner loop, and those lines still get matched when they are next to something distinctive.

The downside is that it silently changes results on long sequences with a small alphabet, most commonly character-level comparison of strings over 200 characters. Nearly every character is then popular, few or no seeds exist, and the matcher can report far less similarity than is really there. An extreme case: with `s = "a"*100 + "b"*100`, `SequenceMatcher(None, "x" + s, s).ratio()` is 0.0, because every element of `b` is popular and the first elements don't line up. With `autojunk=False` it is about 0.998.

**Why it works**

The loop is the Euclidean algorithm on `n/d`, which produces the continued-fraction terms `a` of `self` one at a time. Alongside it, the recurrence `p ← p0 + a*p1`, `q ← q0 + a*q1` builds the convergents: `p1/q1` is the latest one and `p0/q0` the one before. Convergents alternate between being below and above `self`, each is closer than the last, and their denominators grow. The loop stops at the first term whose convergent would have a denominator `q2` over the limit. It always stops before `d` hits zero, because the last convergent is `self` itself, and the early return has already handled the case where its denominator fits.

At that point there are exactly two candidates:

- **`p1/q1`**: the last convergent that fits. It sits on one side of `self`.
- **`(p0 + k*p1)/(q0 + k*q1)`**: a semiconvergent, with `k = (max_denominator - q0)//q1` being the largest step that still fits (so `k < a`). It sits on the other side of `self`, and moves closer to it as `k` grows.

The theorem quoted in the comment says the best approximations from above and from below are always convergents or semiconvergents. So these two are the best lower and best upper bound with denominator at most the limit, and the answer is whichever is closer.

The final `if` makes that comparison in exact integers. The two candidates are `1/(q1*(q0+k*q1))` apart, because consecutive convergents satisfy `p0*q1 - p1*q0 = ±1`. The distance from `p1/q1` to `self` is `d/(q1*self._denominator)`, where `d` is the remainder Euclid has left. So `p1/q1` wins when its distance is at most half the gap, which rearranges to `2*d*(q0+k*q1) <= self._denominator`. The same ±1 identity means both candidates are already in lowest terms, which is why `_from_coprime_ints` can skip the gcd.

**Why not just round**

Rounding needs a denominator chosen in advance: `round(self * q) / q` gives the nearest multiple of `1/q`. The best fraction under a limit rarely has the limit itself as denominator.

The docstring example shows this, using `Fraction('3.141592653589793')` with limit 10:

| Method | Result | Error |
|---|---|---|
| Round to tenths | 31/10 | about 0.042 |
| `limit_denominator(10)` | 22/7 | about 0.0013 |

To get the right answer by rounding you would have to try every denominator from 1 to the limit and keep the best. That is a million iterations at the default limit, versus a number of Euclid steps logarithmic in the denominator for the loop.

The semiconvergent step also matters. With limit 100 the convergents that fit are 3/1 and 22/7 (the next is 333/106). The loop breaks with `k = (100-1)//7 = 14`, giving `(3 + 14*22)/(1 + 14*7) = 311/99`, which is closer than 22/7 and is what the docstring shows. Stopping at the last convergent would have missed it.

**`firstweekday` and `monthdayscalendar`**

It sets which weekday column 0 of each row represents; the day numbers themselves don't change. The month is padded with `(day1 - firstweekday) % 7` zeros in front and enough zeros behind to complete the last week. So changing it shifts every day to a different column, changes how many leading and trailing zeros there are, and can change the number of rows (4 to 6).

One smaller oddity: the `Calendar` property accepts any integer and reduces it mod 7 on read, while the module-level `setfirstweekday()` rejects anything outside 0–6.

**`itermonthdates` at the edges of the year range**

Yes, there is a surprise. It builds a `datetime.date` for the padding days too, and those belong to the neighbouring months, so at the limits of `datetime` they fall out of range:

- **January of year 1:** padding days would be in December of year 0, so `datetime.date` raises `ValueError`. With the default Monday start it happens to work, because 1 January 0001 is a Monday and no padding is needed. Any other `firstweekday` fails.
- **December 9999:** the month ends on a Friday, so any week start other than Saturday needs padding days in year 10000 and raises `ValueError`.
- **The failure is late.** It is a generator, so nothing is raised at the call. For December 9999 you get every valid date first and the exception only when it reaches the trailing padding. `monthdatescalendar` wraps it in `list()`, so there it fails outright.

The other iterators don't have this problem. `itermonthdays`, `itermonthdays2`, `itermonthdays3` and `itermonthdays4` never construct a `date`, and `weekday()` maps out-of-range years onto `2000 + year % 400`, so they work for any year. That is what the "can be used for dates outside of datetime.date range" note on `itermonthdays3` is about.
